mainEntity.name: Does a larger dental implant always perform better?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not necessarily. A larger implant is only appropriate if there is sufficient bone volume and the anatomy of the area supports it. In some regions of the mouth — particularly where bone is narrow or near important structures such as nerves or sinuses — a standard or narrower implant may be more suitable. The goal is to select the size that best fits the individual patient's anatomy, rather than the largest available option. Suitability is always determined through clinical assessment.

mainEntity.name: Can implants fail because of the wrong size?

acceptedAnswer.text: Implant size that is not well matched to available bone and anatomical conditions can contribute to complications, including inadequate osseointegration or peri-implant bone loss over time. However, implant outcomes are influenced by a combination of factors, including bone quality, oral hygiene, patient health, and the precision of surgical placement. Choosing the appropriate size through careful pre-treatment planning helps reduce the risk of size-related complications.

mainEntity.name: What happens if I do not have enough bone for an implant?

acceptedAnswer.text: If imaging reveals that you have insufficient bone volume for a standard implant, your dental team may discuss preparatory procedures such as bone grafting, which adds bone material to the area to create a more suitable foundation. In the upper jaw where bone height is limited, a sinus lift procedure may be considered. Short implants designed specifically for areas of reduced bone height may also be an option in certain cases. Your clinician will explain what may be appropriate for your individual circumstances.

mainEntity.name: How long does it take for a dental implant to integrate with the bone?

acceptedAnswer.text: The osseointegration process typically takes between three and six months, though this varies depending on the individual, the location of the implant, and the quality and volume of the surrounding bone. During this period, the bone gradually bonds with the titanium surface of the implant. Some clinical protocols allow for earlier loading of the implant with a restoration, but the timing is always determined by the clinical team based on assessed stability and healing progress.

mainEntity.name: Is dental implant treatment suitable for everyone?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dental implants are not suitable for all patients. Factors that may affect suitability include the amount of available bone, general health conditions such as uncontrolled diabetes or certain medications that affect bone healing, gum disease, and smoking. Age may also be a consideration, as implant treatment is generally deferred until the jaw has fully developed. A thorough clinical assessment is required to determine whether implant treatment is appropriate for an individual patient.

mainEntity.name: How can I maintain my dental implant for a good long-term outcome?

acceptedAnswer.text: Maintaining your implant involves consistent daily oral hygiene — brushing twice a day, cleaning between implants with interdental brushes or floss, and using any tools recommended by your dental hygienist. Regular professional maintenance appointments are important for monitoring the health of the tissues around the implant. Lifestyle factors such as avoiding smoking and managing any teeth-grinding habits also contribute to long-term implant health. Your dental team can provide personalised guidance based on your specific situation.
